newsitem.title: USA: U.S. Senate confirms Albright and Cohen to Cabinet.
newsitem.headline: U.S. Senate confirms Albright and Cohen to Cabinet.

text.p: The Senate moved swiftly to put President Bill Clinton's new Cabinet in place on Wednesday, confirming Madeleine Albright as secretary of state and former Republican Sen. William Cohen as defence secretary.

Albright will become the first woman to head the state department and Cohen will be Clinton's only Republican Cabinet member. Their confirmation, by 99-0 votes, came two days after Clinton was sworn in for his second term.

A third nominee for the president's national security team, national security adviser Anthony Lake, picked to be CIA director, is more controversial. He is under attack for his role in allowing Iranian arms to flow to the Bosnian Moslems and has become a target of the right.
Seven other high-level nominees also await Senate action.

Clinton called the Senate's quick votes on Albright and Cohen "a strong signal to the world of its determination to work in a constructive and bipartisan spirit with the administation on our nation's foreign policy and national defence." He said in a statement he hoped that would continue.

Albright, 59, succeeds Warren Christopher as secretary of state to become the premier voice in U.S. foreign policy. Cohen, a former member of the Armed Services Committee who retired as senator from Maine at the end of last year, takes over from the highly regarded William Perry.

Albright has been serving as Clinton's ambassador to the United Nations where her stand against reappointment of Boutros Boutros-Ghali as secretary-general won her points with Republican critics of the world body.

Boutros-Ghali's successor arrived in Washington on Wednesday for talks with administration officials and members of Congress on U.N. reforms and payment of the $1.3 billion U.S. debt to the world body.
Known for her forthright speech and avoidance of diplomatic circumlocution, Albright was warmly praised by members of both parties.

Born in Prague, she says her political life was moulded by the diplomatic appeasement of Adolf Hitler at Munich and by the experience of bomb shelters in London where her family fled the Nazi invasion.

The evident high regard in which she is held among members of Congress may well be crucial as she lobbies hard for more funding for the foreign affairs budget, which Christopher complained has been cut to dangerous levels.
At the U.S. mission to the U.N. in New York, Albright told reporters the Senate vote "signals a new era of bipartisan foreign policy and I can't wait to get started."

In Senate debate, Sen Jesse Helms, a North Carolina Republican and chairman of the Senate Foreign Relations Committee, supported Albright's nomination but faulted Clinton's foreign policy over the past four years. He said it had given "a message of weakened resolve around the world."
Helms said that "we'll be watching her closely" to see if Albright had learned from the past "disasters," including U.S. involvement in Somalia and Haiti.
Helms also said he would reintroduce a plan to reorganize the State Department, saying it would save $1 billion a year.
Last year the Clinton administration and Helms were deadlocked for months over his plan to eliminate three foreign policy agencies. Clinton eventually killed it by veto.
Albright, in her testimony to the Foreign Relations Committee, said she had an open mind about the proposal.

Sen Judd Gregg, a New Hampshire Republican, voiced concern that the Clinton administration would seek funds to pay U.S. arrears to the United Nations. He said there had been much talk but little success on reform and "suspect" budget cuts.
